channel.title: Threshold Effects
channel.description: Threshold Effects — essays and research notes by Timothy D. Spivey on mandatory breach disclosure, cybersecurity governance, and the practice of data science.

item.title: Why “Threshold Effects”
item.description: The name comes from econometrics — a relationship that changes character once a variable crosses a critical value. It is also a fair description of everything this blog will be about.

item.title: Gulf Coast: Who the Money Moves Through
item.description: BEAD is finally putting fiber in the ground around northwest Florida and south Alabama. Five years of process decided who gets to build — and it wasn't construction capability that decided.

item.title: A Fair Fight with SOX 404
item.description: Arguing against myself: SOX Section 404 is the strongest counterexample to this series' thesis. The argument survives — but comes out more precise than it went in.

item.title: Say Something vs. Build Something
item.description: There are rules that require organizations to say something and rules that require them to build something. Only the second kind has a track record of changing what organizations are.

item.title: The Dashboard Is Green
item.description: Goodhart's Law and Campbell's Law warned us fifty years ago: the metric changes what the organization reports, not what the organization is. We built the dashboards anyway.

item.title: What the Broadband Labels Revealed
item.description: The FCC's broadband nutrition labels were identical for all 35 ISPs a 2025 study scored. What the mandate produced depended entirely on what each organization already was.

item.title: Wanted: The Best Counterexample
item.description: The honest version of an argument has to survive its best counterexample. So: what's the strongest case of a rule that actually changed what organizations are?

item.title: Three Rules, Same Outcome
item.description: AI governance, compliance programs, mandatory disclosure: three domains, three rules, same outcome. The rule changes what organizations are required to do. It rarely changes what they are.

item.title: Shadow IT Was the Rehearsal
item.description: Shadow IT persisted because unsanctioned tools solved real problems faster than approved ones. AI governance is replaying the same dynamic — in months instead of years.

item.title: Paper Trails and Shadow AI
item.description: Only 37% of compliance leaders can measure whether their programs work — and half the U.S. workforce is using AI at work without knowing if it's allowed. Why did we think a document was going to govern a behavior?

item.title: Cover-Yourself 8-Ks
item.description: When the SEC required four-business-day incident disclosure, firms responded with “cover yourself 8-Ks.” Organizations don't respond to regulatory intent — they respond to regulatory incentives.

item.title: The Faster-Is-Better Assumption
item.description: The assumption behind mandatory breach disclosure timing is that faster equals better. Across 1,054 breach events and three empirical channels, that assumption doesn't hold up well.
